new_entities.name: Heavy menstruation
new_entities.description: Menstrual blood loss heavy enough to impair daily life or cause clinically significant blood loss.

edges.effect_quant: In adolescent cross-sectional data, heavy menstrual bleeding was associated with greater odds of iron deficiency (OR 3.0, 95% CI 2.0 to 4.6).
edges.population: adolescent and reproductive-age females with heavy menstrual bleeding
edges.mechanism: Repeated high menstrual blood loss increases iron losses month after month and can outpace dietary replacement even before anemia appears. That makes ferritin depletion a predictable intermediate outcome, especially when heavy bleeding is combined with low iron intake or other gynecologic pathology.
edges.summary: Heavy menstruation is one of the clearest real-world drivers of iron deficiency in girls and women. Review literature, adolescent clinic cohorts, and newer population data all point the same way: once bleeding is heavy enough to be clinically significant, iron depletion becomes common and often underrecognized before frank anemia is identified.
edges.caveats: The degree of risk depends on bleeding duration, baseline iron intake, and whether iron deficiency is screened with ferritin rather than hemoglobin alone. This edge is strongest for persistent heavy bleeding, not for isolated subjective impressions of a single heavy cycle.

evidence.citation: Barros VV et al 2022 Rev Bras Ginecol Obstet
